A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MuLo-SD research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete supplementary material are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original Tar-1.5B benchmarking, latency measurements, component ablations, and generated-image comparisons, including supplementary experiments.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on Tar-1.5B, Tar-7B, and LlamaGen-XL, alongside ablations, latency breakdowns, and qualitative results.

M1.justification: v2 adds whole-image drafting with ZipAR and parallel resampling across rejection islands, with ZipAR also operating within islands (Section 3.4). It additionally introduces a training-free pixel-space upsampling route and makes it the default. v1 used learned latent up/down-samplers with sequential drafting and resampling.

E1.justification: Both versions retain LAION-COCO-Aesthetic training data, GenEval and DPG-Bench evaluation, and MS-COCO 2017 validation images for perceptual metrics. Text-to-image generation at 512p and 1024p remains the task coverage. Adding Tar-7B and LlamaGen changes model configurations rather than datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: v2 removes Table 1's entire broad cross-model comparison block, including Chameleon, Lumina-mGPT, Transfusion, Show-O, Janus/Janus-Pro, D-DiT, Emu3, and Harmon. The comparison consequently focuses on acceleration within base generators. ZipAR-16, EAGLE-2, and LANTERN remain the principal acceleration comparators and are also evaluated on the added model configurations.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from Tar-1.5B alone to Tar-7B at both resolutions and LlamaGen-XL at 512p. v2 also introduces parallel-versus-sequential evaluations at matched acceptance thresholds. The existing metrics, A100/batch-one timing setup, and supplementary 500-prompt latency protocol remain; the retained latency description still excludes MLLM conditioning time.

E4.justification: Figure 5d adds an ablation testing parallel decoding, and Figure 7 adds component-level latency breakdowns with parallel decoding enabled. Figure 5a removes the DINO-discriminator variant and adds the pixel-space upsampler comparison. Probability-pooling, local-expansion, and supplementary neighborhood-radius ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bands. The revised tables and plots retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces MuLo-SD results with results for the revised default: Tar-1.5B/1024p changes from 1.68x speedup and 76.3 GenEval to 3.90x and 76.8. New Tar-7B/1024p results report 5.33x and 85.4. New LlamaGen results report 1.40x, below LANTERN's 1.59x and ZipAR's 1.88x. These involve changed method configurations; supplementary curves and qualitative outputs are also revised.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 8 newly defines rejection islands as disjoint 8-connected components partitioning the expanded rejection set. Existing acceptance rules, neighborhood definitions, and the theoretical sequential-speedup expression remain mathematically equivalent. No new theorem or proof is supplied.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion elevate parallel-decoding integration from proposed future work to a third central contribution. The headline speedup changes from approximately 1.7x to 5x, and claimed superiority expands from speculative-decoding baselines to parallel decoding, including ZipAR.

C2.justification: New Section 4.5 identifies memory costs from two checkpoints/KV caches and dependence on drafter-verifier distributional alignment, linking weaker LlamaGen gains to this limitation and proposing self-speculation as a remedy. v2 also explains choosing the training-free pixel upsampler despite weaker isolated performance, whereas v1 selected the learned PatchGAN variant for its trade-off.

D1.justification: v2 identifies HIT-SR as the pixel-space super-resolution component. It removes explicit Tar, ZipAR, and LANTERN repository links and v1's training-time/hardware disclosure and hinge-loss, LeCam, and augmentation details. Most learned-sampler architecture, optimizer, batch-size, training-step, and inference-hyperparameter information remains in the supplement; these omissions do not establish changed training procedures.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for connected-component labeling and HIT-SR, while removing works supporting deleted comparisons or training discussion, including ImageFolder and Projected GANs. ZipAR is repositioned as an implemented component rather than only a prospective combination. The broader positioning relative to LANTERN and multi-scale autoregressive models remains substantially intact.

P1.justification: v2 condenses the preliminaries and multi-scale motivation, separates implementation details from experimental settings, and introduces parallel-decoding and limitations subsections. Much wording and the overall introduction–related work–method–experiments–conclusion–supplement structure remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Table 1 is reorganized around generator/resolution configurations. Figure 3 is redrawn to show rejection islands, Figure 4 expands from six to eight examples, Figure 5 gains a fourth panel, and Figure 7 becomes a sequential/parallel four-panel comparison. Figure 8 changes axis ranges, qualitative displays are refreshed, and document typography changes throughout.

improvement.justification: v2 turns v1's proposed remedy for sequential bottlenecks into a specified, experimentally tested contribution, supported by the new parallel-decoding ablation and component timings. Broader model validation, a training-free variant, and explicit memory/alignment limitations substantially strengthen practical relevance and evidential scope. Reporting remains imperfect: Appendix Section 8 retains the old ZipAR-dominance interpretation, some Table 1 deltas contradict their absolute values, and claims of consistent superiority overreach the LlamaGen results. These defects temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in validation and applicability analysis.
